planting.note: Scarify or use fresh seed since the hard seed coat causes erratic germination, then let the stand build root reserves for a full season before the first light grazing or mow-and-drop cutting.

directions: Broadcast or drill scarified seed at a modest rate into clean, low-fertility, acidic soils where few other forage legumes persist, since this shrubby stylo is valued precisely for thriving where better soils are unavailable. Once established, its deep taproot and heavy leaf litter slowly rebuild organic matter and fix nitrogen for companion grasses growing alongside it. Allow a full season of uninterrupted growth before the first graze or mow so plants can build woody reserves, then manage with periodic hard cutting to keep the stand productive for several years.
sources: Tropical Forages (CSIRO, Qld DAF, CIAT, ILRI)

planting.note: Broadcast or drill into a clean, warm seedbed alongside a companion grass, since burgundy bean tolerates heavier, more alkaline soils than siratro and recovers well after mowing or grazing.

directions: Drill or broadcast Cadarga seed into a warm, weed-suppressed seedbed at a light rate, pairing it with a companion grass so the trailing stems have something to climb for better light capture. The legume's extensive root system and heavy leaf drop build soil nitrogen and organic matter season after season as a long-lived perennial component of a pasture or cover mix. Mow or graze it down periodically rather than letting it go to seed unchecked, since burgundy bean spreads readily once a stand matures.
sources: Tropical Forages (CSIRO, Qld DAF, CIAT, ILRI)

planting.note: Inoculate seed before sowing and keep the stand mowed or lightly grazed, since this stoloniferous clover forms a dense living mulch that tolerates part-day shade better than white clover.

directions: Sow inoculated seed thinly over a firm, moist seedbed in full sun to light shade, where this stoloniferous clover spreads outward to knit together a dense, mat-forming living mulch. Like other clovers it fixes atmospheric nitrogen through root nodules, steadily enriching the soil beneath tree crops or open pasture alike. Keep it mowed or lightly grazed rather than letting surrounding vegetation overtop it, since its creeping growth habit depends on regular light reaching the crown.
sources: Tropical Forages (CSIRO, Qld DAF, CIAT, ILRI)

planting.note: Nick or hot-water-soak the hard seed coat before sowing, then cut the shrubby stand back hard before it sets heavy seed and dig or mow the nitrogen-rich foliage into the bed as a green-manure mulch.

directions: Pretreat the hard seed coat before broadcasting or direct-sowing into a warm bed, since untreated seed germinates slowly and unevenly. The fast-growing shrub produces an enormous volume of nitrogen-rich leafy biomass within its first season, making it a favored intercrop for rebuilding depleted soil ahead of a following crop. Cut the stand back hard before woody stems dominate and before heavy seed set, then chop and dig the trimmings into the bed as a green-manure mulch rather than leaving them to decompose on the surface.

planting.note: Broadcast thickly into a warm, well-drained seedbed where few other legumes will establish, then mow or disk the trailing vines in at first flower to return fixed nitrogen before they set hard seed.

directions: Broadcast seed at a generous rate into a warm, well-drained bed, since this fast-establishing trailing legume is typically grown as a short-cycle green manure rather than a long-season crop. Its dense low groundcover suppresses weeds quickly while fixing nitrogen in root nodules through the heat of summer. Mow, disk, or turn the vines under at first flowering to capture peak nitrogen content before the plant hardens off and sets seed.

planting.note: Sow the fine seed shallowly into a firm, weed-free bed since seedlings are slow and easily shaded out, then begin the first cut or graze once clumps reach full height to encourage tillering and deep rooting.

directions: Sow the small, fluffy seed shallowly into a firm, weed-free bed, since seedlings are slow to establish and easily outcompeted by faster weeds in the first weeks. Once tillered out, this tufted perennial grass produces a deep, fibrous root mass that stabilizes soil and recycles nutrients cycled up from lower soil layers. Begin regular mowing or grazing once stands reach full height to keep regrowth palatable and to prevent the clumps from becoming rank and woody.
sources: Tropical Forages (CSIRO, Qld DAF, CIAT, ILRI)
